title: Summer robe (hito-e) with cranes and pines

altText: A light summer kimono of thin silk, patterned with cranes and pine trees in a design made by resist-dyeing.

context: A summer robe, called a hito-e, made in Japan around the 1870s to 1880s, during the Meiji period. It is plain-weave silk decorated with paste-resist dyeing and shows cranes and pines. Both are traditional symbols of long life.

descriptions.k: This is a light robe for summer. It is made from silk. Birds called cranes and pine trees are on it. In Japan, they are signs of a long, happy life. Which part of the robe do you like best?
descriptions.g12: This summer robe from Japan is made of thin silk so that it stays cool. It shows cranes and pine trees. In Japan, both stand for a long life. The artist used a paste to keep dye away from some parts of the cloth. Where do you see the birds and the trees?
descriptions.g35: A hito-e is an unlined summer kimono, made from thin cloth to stay cool in the heat. This one was made in Japan in the 1870s or 1880s, and it shows cranes and pines, which symbolize long life. The design was made by paste-resist dyeing, where paste blocks dye from chosen areas. Why might a robe for hot weather have such a happy, lucky design?
descriptions.g68: Made in the early Meiji period, this hito-e is an unlined summer robe in plain-weave silk, decorated by paste-resist dyeing. Cranes and pines are auspicious motifs, standing for long life and good fortune. The design also needs to work on a garment, wrapping around a moving body. Look at how the motifs are placed over the surface. How does a traditional pattern feel in a changing era, when Japan was opening to new influences?
descriptions.g910: This summer robe dates from the 1870s and 1880s, a period of rapid change in Japan, yet its imagery of cranes and pines draws on long-established symbols of longevity. Paste-resist dyeing on plain-weave silk produces crisp areas of color without heavy surface texture, suiting a lightweight summer garment. Consider how pattern placement works across a garment, and how traditional symbols persist or are reinterpreted when a society is changing.
descriptions.g1112: As a Meiji-period garment, this hito-e sits between continuity and change. Cranes and pines are among the most durable auspicious motifs in East Asian art, and their appearance here shows how long-standing visual languages continued even as Japan modernized. Paste-resist dyeing shows the sophistication of textile workshops. Museums display robes statically, whereas such garments were meant to be seen in motion and in the seasonal context of summer. How should we read tradition and modernity in dress?

teacherNote.context: A summer kimono (hito-e) from the early Meiji period, ca. 1870 to 1880s, in plain-weave silk with paste-resist dyeing. Cranes and pines are traditional symbols of longevity.
directions: Ask students to design a pattern of symbols for a wish and explain why they chose them.
Compare this summer robe with the spring kosode in the archive: what changes between seasons?
Discuss how tradition and change can exist side by side in clothing.
